title: "Real-time joint estimation of the size of the 2026 Bundibugyo virus outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo"

abstract: |
  An outbreak of Ebola disease caused by Bundibugyo virus is ongoing in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, with exported cases in Uganda.
  Most infections are unreported, so the current size of the outbreak has to be inferred from the surveillance counts that are published.
  Published estimates use a subset of those counts under fixed delay, doubling-time and case-fatality assumptions.
  We instead fit every count the national situation reports publish in one posterior, refitted and released with each data update.
  One latent infection process by province, staged through explicit delays and stream-specific ascertainment, generates every stream.
  The cumulative counts are fitted as the increments between reports, with a fitted level offset where reporting changed, and streams that stop being reported stay in the likelihood.
  The model began as a reproduction of an early export-based estimate and became a renewal model with a time-varying reproduction number and provincial structure.
  We evaluate each release by one-week-ahead forecasts scored against the data that arrive next and against a persistence baseline, by fits to single streams, and against the published estimates.
  At the release analysed the joint model estimates an outbreak substantially larger than the confirmed count, with transmission continuing.
  Persistence is hard to beat one week ahead, and the joint forecast beat it at most releases only for the onset curve.
  The joint estimate sits at the low end of the range that the single streams imply on their own, and the interval on size is no narrower than the priors on ascertainment and delays that the data do not move.
  A joint estimate from published reports alone is feasible in real time and makes the agreement and conflict between surveillance streams explicit.
